analysis.one_liner: Creates public financing for congressional elections and sharply boosts matching funds for small presidential donations.
analysis.headline: The Empowering Citizens Act never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the presidential public financing system so that a small donation of $250 or less is matched with six public dollars, and it would create, for the first time, public financing for House and Senate campaigns. Candidates who take the public money would have to accept tighter contribution limits, take no bundled donations from lobbyists, and stay out of fundraising for super PACs. The money would come from taxpayers voluntarily checking a box on their returns and from optional direct donations. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and small-dollar donors gain the most: their $25 or $100 gifts would count six times as much against candidates who opt in. Candidates without access to wealthy networks, large bundled contributions, or super PAC money could compete using broad grassroots support, and voters get more candidates who are not financed through lobbyist bundling.

how_it_helps.text: The bill multiplies the presidential primary match from one public dollar per small contribution to six dollars per contribution of $250 or less, so a $100 donation delivers $600 to a participating candidate [S2].

It creates a new public financing program for House and Senate candidates who show real grassroots support, paying a six-to-one match on qualified contributions up to a ceiling of $2 million for a House candidate and $10 million for a Senate candidate [S2][S3].

Candidates who join the program cannot accept contributions bundled by registered lobbyists and cannot solicit, receive, or direct funds for super PACs that ignore federal contribution limits [S2][S3].

It strengthens disclosure of bundled contributions, requiring campaigns to report lobbyists and other bundlers who aggregate more than $15,000 in bundled gifts to congressional committees or $50,000 to presidential campaigns [S3].
It closes the joint fundraising committee channel, which lets candidates and party committees collect checks far larger than the normal per-donor limits in one place [S3].

It loosens the flow of money to candidates who opt in by raising the coordinated spending a national party can make on behalf of its presidential candidate to $100 million, adjusted for inflation, and by letting parties spend without limit for participating congressional candidates when the money comes from small donors [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on taxpayers who choose to participate: the check-off for the Presidential Election Campaign Fund would rise from $3 to $20 per person, and taxpayers could donate extra amounts on their returns. For the first cycle, the Treasury would lend the fund repayable advances. Candidates outside the program, large donors, super PAC operators, and incumbents built on big-check fundraising would bear the cost of adjusting to a system where small donations matter far more.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voluntary taxpayer check-offs and big-money fundraisers

drawbacks.text: The public financing is funded through the tax check-off, which would rise from $3 to $20 per return, plus optional donations; the fund has historically run short, and the bill authorizes repayable Treasury advances to cover the first presidential cycle [S2][S3].

While boosting public matching funds, the bill repeals the existing spending limits that came with old-style public financing for presidential primaries and general elections, which could increase total campaign spending [S2][S3].

The entry requirements are steep: a presidential candidate would have to raise $25,000 in each of 20 states, and a House candidate would need 400 in-district donors and $40,000 to qualify, thresholds that favor organized major-party campaigns and can lock out minor-party or late-starting candidates [S2][S3].

The ban on candidates soliciting money for super PACs was already legally fragile after court decisions expanded independent spending rights, so a court challenge could have stripped that provision even if the bill passed (general knowledge, not in the provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest in dollars: candidates would answer to many small donors rather than a few large ones, paid for by taxpayers who opt in through the check-off and voluntary donations, plus temporary Treasury advances. The honest objections are that the qualifying thresholds tilt the system toward established major-party candidates, that repealing spending limits while adding public money could increase total spending, and that the super PAC provision might not survive a court challenge. The design is defensible, not perfect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees, House Administration and Ways and Means, for the entire two-year Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative David Price of North Carolina introduced the bill on January 21, 2015, together with Representative Chris Van Hollen of Maryland [S1][S3].
Six House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Speaker sent the bill to two committees at once, House Administration and Ways and Means, splitting jurisdiction between them [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral, through the end of the 114th Congress in January 2017 [S5].
Under the bill, a $250-or-less donation to a participating presidential candidate would be matched with six public dollars, up to $300 million in total primary payments [S2].
The bill would have established the first public financing program for congressional elections, drawing from the existing voluntary taxpayer check-off fund [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of both parties, large donors, lobbyist bundlers, and super PAC operators keep the existing fundraising system unchanged. Small donors and candidates without access to big-money networks gained nothing from the two years the bill sat untouched.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so the only recorded partisan fact is that a bill backed solely by Democrats died without action under Republican committee control.

industries.industry: Super PACs and large outside spending groups
industries.note: The bill would bar federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting, receiving, or directing funds to super PACs that ignore contribution limits, cutting the line between campaigns and unlimited outside money. Groups built to accept unlimited checks would lose that access to the politicians they support.

Participating candidates could not accept lobbyist-bundled contributions, joint fundraising committees would be banned outright, and bundlers above set thresholds would have to be disclosed by name and employer. Their influence rests on aggregating many checks, which the bill targets directly.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders and national party committees
industries.note: Participating candidates would face a $1,000 contribution cap, personal spending limits, and restrictions on raising money for party committees, reducing incumbent fundraising advantages. But parties would gain the ability to spend without limit for participating candidates when the money comes from donations of $1,000 or less, and the presidential coordinated-spending cap rises to $100 million.

industries.industry: Taxpayers who opt into the check-off
industries.note: The check-off rises from $3 to $20 per return, and taxpayers may add voluntary donations, so participation remains a choice; the fund would also receive repayable Treasury advances for the first cycle. Those who participate pay more in exchange for the public financing the program funds.
